name: Locks of Love style hair donation

card.summary: Growing hair long, then cutting and donating it to make wigs for children, giving the donor a fresh haircut and a shorter, easier style.
card.note: Charities set minimum lengths (Locks of Love asks for at least 10 inches).

quick.overview:
Hair donation means growing hair out and cutting it for a charity that makes wigs for children with hair loss. For the donor, the appeal is a style reset: a long-hair phase, then a cut into a shorter look.

Locks of Love, founded in 1997, popularised the practice in the United States. It requires donated hair to be at least 10 inches long.
quick.how: People grow hair to the required length, tie it in ponytails or braids, have it cut by a stylist, and send it to the charity. Many then keep a shorter style.
quick.risks: Few physical risks. Donors should know the length rules and that much donated hair is sold rather than used in wigs, per the charity.

lead: Locks of Love-style hair donation is the practice of growing out hair and cutting it for donation to a charity that makes hairpieces for children with medical hair loss. For donors it doubles as a haircut project, ending in a shorter, lower-maintenance style.[1]

Locks of Love was founded on May 28, 1997 by Madonna Coffman, a nurse who had alopecia, and is based in West Palm Beach, Florida. It makes wigs for disadvantaged children up to age 21 affected by alopecia, burns or cancer treatment, and requires donated hair of at least 10 inches.[1]

Coverage in 2013 raised questions about hair valuations; Snopes attributed the figures to difficulty valuing hair. The charity said in 2007 that about 80 percent of donated hair was unsuitable for wigs and the rest was sold to fund its work.[1]

angle.text: The donor gets a planned cut and a visible style change; the charity receives hair for wigs.

paras: Locks of Love was founded in 1997 and received IRS 501(c)(3) status in December 1997.[1]

In 2013 Forbes and the Huffington Post reported that up to $6 million of donated hair was unaccounted for yearly; Snopes attributed the discrepancy to valuation difficulty and found no black-market income in tax filings.[1] The IRS treats hair as a body part, so donating it is not tax-deductible, though the haircut cost may be.[1]
Forum users on T Nation occasionally mention growing hair to donate or shaving for a relative in treatment, usually as passing remarks.

timeline.event: Locks of Love founded in Florida.[1]
Charity says about 80 percent of donated hair is unsuitable for wigs.[1]
